title: The Pollutant We Can't Close Our Ears To
focus: Complex noun phrases and careful use of associated with / caused by

lines.text: Good morning. Noise is the pollutant we've learned to live with, and I'd like to suggest that we've learned it rather too well.
Most of us think of noise as an annoyance. The research points to something more serious: long-term exposure to road and aircraft noise is associated with sleep disturbance and raised blood pressure.
Notice the wording there. Associated with is not the same as caused by, and the researchers are careful about that distinction.
Even so, the evidence has become strong enough that international health bodies have issued guidelines recommending limits on night-time noise.
What makes noise unusual is that you can't close your ears. During sleep, the brain keeps monitoring sound, and loud events can trigger a stress response even when you don't wake up.
That's why a person may believe they've adapted to a noisy street, while their body tells a different story.
Now, who is most affected? Often it's lower-income households, which tend to be located near busy roads, railways and airports. This is a pattern that has been repeated in many cities.
There's also an effect on children. Studies of schools under flight paths have found poorer reading performance, although it's difficult to separate noise from other disadvantages.
So what can be done? Quieter road surfaces, lower speed limits and better insulation all help, but none is a complete solution.
Interestingly, there's a psychological dimension. A sound that you can control, or that you consider meaningful, bothers you less than one that is imposed.
A neighbour's party that you've been invited to is tolerable, whereas the same music at the same volume, uninvited, is unbearable.
This has implications for planning. Residents who feel consulted about changes tend to be less annoyed than those who are simply informed.
My conclusion is that quiet should be treated as a public good, rather than a luxury available to those who can afford a house in a calm street.
For next week, please read the two articles on noise mapping and think about what a fair noise limit might look like in your own city.

title: Refills and Valuations
focus: Hedging and tentative language (I'd be inclined to, it may be worth, we'd probably want)

lines.text: Leila, I've read your plan. I'm impressed by the product, though I have some doubts about the valuation.
I'm glad you raised it. What concerns you?
You're asking for a figure that assumes sales will double each year. I'd be inclined to say that's optimistic.
It might be, but we've had that growth for two years, and our repeat customers are rising.
That's encouraging. Still, repeat purchases of cleaning products can fall away once the novelty fades. It may be worth testing that before we commit.
Fair. We could share the retention data from the last eighteen months, which might reassure you.
That would help. Now, on the terms, we'd probably want a seat on the board.
I'd have thought that was reasonable. My hesitation is more about control. I'd prefer to keep the final say on product decisions.
I can see that. Perhaps we could agree that you decide on product, and we have a voice on spending above a certain level.
That seems like a workable compromise, although I'd want the level to be set high enough that I'm not asking permission for ordinary purchases.
I'd be open to that. What would you say to a smaller investment now, with more to follow if you meet your targets?
Hmm. That might actually suit us. A smaller sum would mean giving away less of the company at the start.
Exactly. It would also protect us if the growth turned out slower than hoped.
I'd be happy to explore it. Could you send me a draft so my lawyer can look at it?
Of course. I'd expect to have something to you by early next week.

title: Everyone Can Be a Scientist
focus: Gerunds as subjects and abstract noun phrases

lines.text: Welcome to Open Questions. Today, citizen science, meaning ordinary people helping to collect or analyse scientific data. Tariq, how big is this?
Bigger than most people realise. Counting birds in gardens, recording the dates of first blossom, even classifying photographs of galaxies, volunteers do all of it.
Isn't there a risk that amateurs make mistakes?
There is, and being honest about that is part of the method. Checking records against each other and asking experts to review unusual sightings catches many errors.
So the data's reliable?
For many questions, surprisingly so. Gathering information across a whole country would be impossible for a small team, so the sheer number of observations compensates for individual slips.
What can't volunteers do?
Designing the study, mostly, and interpreting results with caution. Knowing what question to ask is a skill that takes years.
Does the project benefit the volunteers too?
Often. Taking part in real research gives people a sense of purpose, and some have gone on to study the subject properly.
I'm slightly cynical, I'll admit. Isn't it a cheap way for scientists to get free labour?

That's a legitimate worry, and good projects take it seriously. Sharing results with the volunteers, crediting them in papers, and responding to their questions are what separate partnership from exploitation.
Can you give an example of something volunteers found that surprised the experts?
In one galaxy project, a volunteer noticed an odd glowing blob that the scientists hadn't expected. Following it up led to a published study, and the object is now named after her.
Wonderful. So, anyone with a phone and a free afternoon?
Pretty much. Finding a project that suits your interests is the first step.

title: Classrooms Behind Bars
focus: Passive and infinitive structures (need + -ing, be due to, be to come out)

lines.text: Today's panel asks whether prisons should invest more in education. Mr Reid, you run a prison. What's your view?
That it's long overdue. Many of the people in my prison left school early, and their reading needs improving before anything else can be attempted.
The research I'm familiar with suggests that people who take part in education while in prison are less likely to reoffend. Of course, it can't be said for certain that education is the cause.
Why might that be, Doctor Asante?
Partly skills, which open doors to jobs. But partly identity. Being treated as a student rather than only as an offender changes how a person sees themselves.
I'd second that. I've watched men who'd never opened a book discover that they could write, and it altered how they carried themselves.
Is public opinion a barrier? Some say prisoners shouldn't be given advantages.
That's an argument I hear often. My answer is that most prisoners are due to be released, and the question is what kind of person is to come out.
Precisely. Education isn't a reward; it's an investment in public safety. The cost needs weighing against the cost of reoffending.
But is there enough money?
Not at present. Classrooms need updating, and teachers are hard to recruit, partly because the work isn't seen as attractive.
Technology could be part of the answer, although it needs to be handled carefully. Secure tablets could let people study at their own pace.
I'd welcome that, provided security isn't compromised. The idea is to extend access, not to create loopholes.
Is there a risk of treating education as a quick fix?
Certainly. A course is not going to transform a life by itself. Housing and employment on release are just as important, and are often neglected.
I'd agree. Education has to be followed up outside the gate, otherwise the effect fades.
Thank you both.

title: My Grandmother's Handful

lines.text: Marisol, you've been collecting your grandmother's recipes for years. How did it start?
I've been writing them down since she became ill. She never measured anything, so I've spent a great deal of time watching her hands and asking questions.
What does a recipe without measurements look like?
Like a conversation. A handful of this, until it smells right. I've learned to translate that into numbers, but something is always lost.
Have you been cooking her food in your restaurant?
Some of it, though I've changed my mind about that several times. At first I thought it was disrespectful to alter anything. Lately I've been thinking that cooking is a living tradition.
Her region is famous for potatoes, isn't it?
Yes. The potato comes from the Andes, and there are thousands of varieties, many of which you've probably never heard of. I've tried to cook with as many as I can find.
Is that hard?
It's become harder. Some varieties have been disappearing because farmers find it more profitable to grow just a few.
And your grandmother, what does she make of it?
She's been laughing at me, honestly. She says the only way to learn is to cook for people, not to write about it.
Has the project changed you?
Enormously. I've become much more patient, and I've started cooking dishes like chuño, a freeze-dried potato, that I'd always considered old-fashioned.
Will there be a book?
I've been working on one for two years now, and I think it's nearly finished. Though my grandmother will have the final word.
I hope she approves.
She's already told me that the pictures make her look too serious.

title: Handing Over the Wheel
focus: Future forms (be bound to, be set to, be likely to, be about to)

lines.text: Tonight: are self-driving cars set to make our roads safer? Doctor Chen?
I think they're bound to, eventually. Most accidents result from human error, and a machine that never gets tired or distracted should, in principle, do better.
In principle. But I'd say we're a long way off. These systems are likely to struggle with unusual situations, like roadworks or a police officer waving traffic through.
That's true now, but the technology is improving, and I'd expect the gap to narrow considerably over the next decade.
Mr Bailey, are you saying the technology can't improve?
No. I'm saying that the transition is the dangerous bit. For years we'll have a mixture of human drivers and machines, and the two don't predict each other well.
That's a fair point. Though I'd argue that this is exactly when the accident figures are most likely to be studied carefully.
Studied, yes, but at what cost? If there are fatal accidents in the meantime, public trust is bound to take a knock.
It might, though we already accept a great many deaths on the roads today without much alarm. A machine's mistakes simply feel different.
Which is a psychological point, not a technical one. People forgive human error more readily than machine error.
So what needs to happen for the public to accept them?
Transparent testing, independent safety reports, and clear rules about who is responsible when something goes wrong.
I'd add that nobody should be forced to give up driving. There'll always be people who prefer to be in control.
I'd agree. I don't think that anyone is about to ban human drivers, nor should they.
A thoughtful note to end on. Thank you both.

title: Three Myths About Sign Language
focus: Correcting and contrasting (far from it, not so much… as, rather than)

lines.text: Good morning. I'd like to begin by dismissing three myths about sign languages, because you'll meet all of them in everyday conversation.

The first myth is that sign language is universal. Far from it. British Sign Language and American Sign Language are mutually unintelligible, even though the spoken languages of the two countries are the same.

The second myth is that sign language is a simplified version of the spoken language, a kind of gesture code. It isn't. It has its own grammar, which is not so much a translation of English as a different system altogether.

In signing, for example, space is used to show relationships. A signer can place a person on their left and then refer back to that spot, which is something that spoken English does with pronouns, only less elegantly.

The third myth is that it can't express abstract ideas. In fact, people have given academic lectures and written poetry in sign languages, and the poetry makes use of rhythm and handshape the way spoken poetry uses rhyme.
What I find most striking is the story of Nicaraguan Sign Language. In the late nineteen-seventies and the nineteen-eighties, deaf children were brought together in schools for the first time.
They arrived with only simple home gestures. Within a few years, the children had developed a language with consistent grammar, and each new cohort made it richer.
This suggests that language isn't so much taught as grown. Given the chance to communicate, human beings build structure almost instinctively.
Now, it would be wrong to romanticise this. Many deaf children are born to hearing parents who don't sign, and they may reach school without any language at all.
The consequences can be serious, since early exposure to a first language matters for later learning, whether spoken or signed.
That's why many experts argue for early access to sign language rather than treating it as a last resort.
Others, to be fair, worry that this might discourage spoken language. Yet the evidence doesn't generally suggest that signing prevents speech; if anything, it gives children a foundation to build on.
I'd put it like this: the question isn't signing or speaking, but whether a child has a language at all.
For the seminar, please watch a short film in sign language with subtitles, and notice what you can understand without the captions.

title: Fighting Fire with Fire
focus: Third conditional and expressing regret about the past

lines.text: Good afternoon. I want to talk about fire, and in particular about how a century of trying to stamp it out has made many landscapes more dangerous.

For a long time, the policy in many countries was simple: put out every fire as quickly as possible. It seemed sensible. If a fire had been allowed to burn, people thought, it would have caused unnecessary damage.
But many forests are adapted to fire. Small fires clear dead wood and undergrowth, and if those fires are suppressed, fuel accumulates year after year.
Then, when a fire finally starts in dry, windy conditions, it's far more intense. Had the earlier fires been allowed to burn, there would have been less fuel for the large one.
That's the paradox. By preventing small fires, we may have made large ones more likely.
Indigenous communities in Australia, and elsewhere, understood this long before scientists did. They used low-intensity fires, set at the right time of year, to manage the land.
This is sometimes called cultural burning. The fires are cool, slow and patchy, so that animals can escape and the ground isn't scorched.
If governments had listened to these communities earlier, many landscapes might look quite different today. I think that's a fair thing to say, although it's impossible to prove.
Now, I don't want to oversimplify. Cultural burning isn't a cure-all, particularly in a hotter and drier climate, where even a carefully planned burn can escape.
Nor can it be done everywhere. Near towns, the risk of smoke and escape means that other methods, such as thinning vegetation, are needed.
What is changing is the attitude of agencies. Many now work in partnership with traditional owners, and some have admitted that they should have done so sooner.
It's a good example of a wider lesson. If we'd asked the people who lived on the land, we might have avoided some expensive mistakes.
I'd like you to consider what other policies might be reconsidered if we took local knowledge more seriously.
For next week, read the case study on fire management and prepare two questions.

title: In Defence of Boredom

lines.text: Welcome to Small Ideas. Today I'd like to defend something unfashionable: boredom. Doctor Greer, am I mad?
Not at all. Boredom has a terrible reputation, but I'd argue that it's a signal, like hunger, telling us that something is missing.
Missing what?
Meaning, mostly. We're bored when we want to be engaged and can't find anything worth engaging with. That's uncomfortable, and discomfort has always been a spur to action.
Isn't it easier to reach for the phone?
Easier, yes. Better, rarely. Every time we fill a gap with a screen, we deny ourselves a chance to find out what we actually want.
That's quite a claim.

It's a hypothesis, I'll admit. But there's some evidence that people who are given a dull task tend to become more creative afterwards. Boredom seems to send the mind wandering, and wandering is often where ideas come from.
Where's the catch?
The catch is that not all boredom is equal. There's the pleasant drifting kind, and then there's the kind that's stuck in a job with no purpose, which is damaging.
So the same word covers a lot.
Too much, and that's a problem. A child staring out of a window and an employee with nothing to do aren't having the same experience.
How do we give children the useful kind?
By resisting the urge to fill every hour. We schedule children's lives so tightly that we leave no room for them to be bored, and no room for them to become inventive.
Is that really a parenting question, or a political one?
Both. Parents need time, schools need space, and society needs to stop equating busyness with value.
Busy isn't the same as productive.
Exactly. Nor is quiet the same as empty.
A good place to stop. Thank you.
